categories.massacre: Mass killing and destruction of peoples
categories.harm: Texts later used to justify harm

stances.commanded: Commanded by God or a leader in the text
stances.reported: Reported; the text's judgment is unclear or implied
stances.condemned: Condemned or punished within the text

items.title: Lot offers his daughters to a mob
items.what: When the men of Sodom demand Lot's guests, Lot offers his two virgin daughters to the crowd instead.
views: Hospitality to guests outweighed protecting daughters in that culture; the text reports it without praise
Lot's later disgrace (19:30–38) is read by some as an implied judgment
Feminist readings name it a 'text of terror'

items.title: Lot's daughters and their father
items.what: Lot's daughters make him drunk and conceive by him; the children become the ancestors of Moab and Ammon.
views: Explains the origins of Israel's neighbours, often read as a polemic against them
Lot is portrayed as passive and shamed

items.title: Dinah and the massacre at Shechem
items.what: Shechem takes and violates Dinah. Her brothers Simeon and Levi then kill all the men of the city and take the women and children as plunder.
views: Jacob rebukes the killing (34:30) and curses Simeon and Levi's violence (49:5–7)
Dinah never speaks in the story

items.title: Hagar given to Abram
items.what: Sarai gives her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abram to bear a child; when Hagar conceives, Sarai treats her harshly and she flees.
views: A legal custom of the ancient Near East (compare Bilhah, Gen 30:3–4)
God meets Hagar in the wilderness and she gives him a name, El Roi (16:13)

items.title: The Levite's concubine
items.what: A Levite hands his concubine to a mob in Gibeah, who abuse her through the night. She dies; he cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them through Israel.
views: The book frames this as the low point of an age when 'there was no king in Israel' (19:1; 21:25)
Leads to civil war against Benjamin (Judg 20)

items.title: Wives for Benjamin: Jabesh-gilead and Shiloh
items.what: Israel kills the people of Jabesh-gilead except 400 virgin girls, who are given to the Benjamites; others are told to seize young women dancing at Shiloh.
views: Part of the same 'no king' framing; the repair of one atrocity by another
Read by many as deliberate irony by the narrator

items.title: David and Bathsheba
items.what: King David sends for Bathsheba, the wife of one of his soldiers, and sleeps with her; when she becomes pregnant he arranges her husband Uriah's death in battle.
views: Nathan's parable condemns David (2 Sam 12:1–14)
Debated whether Bathsheba could refuse a king; many now read it as abuse of power

items.title: Amnon and Tamar
items.what: David's son Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar, then throws her out.
views: Tamar calls it folly (13:12); David is angry but does nothing (13:21), and Absalom later kills Amnon
Read as the fulfilment of Nathan's judgment on David's house

items.title: Absalom and his father's concubines
items.what: On advice, Absalom sleeps with David's ten concubines publicly to show his break with his father.
views: Fulfils the judgment of 2 Sam 12:11
The women are later confined for life (20:3)

items.title: Midianite captives: kill the boys, keep the virgin girls
items.what: Moses orders the soldiers to kill every male child and every woman who has lain with a man, and to keep the virgin girls alive "for yourselves".
views: Punishment for Midian's role at Baal-peor (Num 25)
Defenders read 'for yourselves' as servants or wives, not abuse; critics read it as sanctioned sexual captivity
Many scholars see it as a later idealised war narrative

items.title: Taking a captive woman as a wife
items.what: A soldier may take a captive woman he desires as a wife after a month of mourning; if he later does not want her, he must let her go free and may not sell her.
views: Defenders: limits on wartime practice compared with surrounding cultures
Critics: consent is absent; it regulates rather than forbids taking captives

items.title: A rapist pays the father and marries the girl
items.what: A man who seizes an unbetrothed virgin and lies with her must pay her father fifty shekels, marry her, and may never divorce her.
views: Some translations read it as seduction rather than force (compare Exod 22:16–17)
Intended to protect a woman's future in a society where she could not otherwise marry
Critics: the woman's wishes are not considered

items.title: A betrothed woman who did not cry out
items.what: If a betrothed woman lies with a man in a town, both are stoned, she because she 'cried not'; in the field, only the man dies, because no one could have heard her.
views: The law presumes consent from silence in a town
The field case is read as recognising that she may have been forced

items.title: Young women gathered for the king
items.what: Officers gather young virgins from across the empire into the Persian king's harem; each spends one night with him.
views: The story critiques Persian excess with irony
Esther rises within a system she did not choose

items.title: Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife stripped and punished
items.what: The prophets picture God's judgment on Jerusalem and Samaria as a husband exposing and punishing an unfaithful wife, with violent sexual imagery.
views: A metaphor for covenant betrayal, not instructions
Critics warn the imagery has been used to excuse domestic abuse

items.title: "Save alive nothing that breatheth"
items.what: Israel is commanded to utterly destroy the nations of Canaan, show them no mercy, and in their cities leave nothing that breathes alive.
views: Judgment on Canaanite practices such as child sacrifice (Deut 12:31)
Hyperbolic war language common in ancient texts (the same peoples remain later, Judg 1)
Archaeology suggests a gradual settlement, not a sudden conquest
Others conclude it is a genuine moral problem in Scripture

items.title: Jericho
items.what: Israel destroys everyone in Jericho, men and women, young and old, and the animals; only Rahab's family is spared.
views: See the herem command (Deut 7, 20)

items.title: "He utterly destroyed all that breathed"
items.what: Joshua's southern and northern campaigns are summarised as leaving no survivors, 'as the LORD God of Israel commanded'.
views: Stylised summary formulas; later chapters list peoples not driven out (Josh 13:13; 15:63)

items.title: Amalek: "slay both man and woman, infant and suckling"
items.what: Samuel tells Saul that God commands the destruction of Amalek, including infants and livestock. Saul spares the king and the best animals and is rejected as king for it.
views: Punishment for Amalek's attack on Israel in the wilderness (Exod 17; Deut 25:17–19)
Amalekites still appear later (1 Sam 30), suggesting hyperbole
Often cited as the hardest command in the Old Testament

items.title: War against Midian
items.what: Israel kills the men and kings of Midian and burns their cities; Moses is angry that the women were spared (31:14–15).
views: See also the captives entry (Num 31:17–18)

items.title: The Flood
items.what: Every living thing on the earth dies except those in the ark.
views: Judgment on universal violence (Gen 6:11–13)
God's promise never to do it again (Gen 8:21; 9:11)

items.title: The death of Egypt's firstborn
items.what: At midnight the LORD kills the firstborn of Egypt, from Pharaoh's son to the prisoner's, and the firstborn of the cattle.
views: Mirrors Pharaoh's killing of Hebrew boys (Exod 1:22)
Questions about punishing children for a ruler's choices

items.title: The priests of Nob
items.what: At Saul's order, Doeg kills 85 priests and everyone in their town, including women, children and infants.
views: Presented as Saul's crime; David takes responsibility (22:22)

items.title: David's treatment of the Ammonites
items.what: The KJV says David 'put them under saws, and under harrows of iron' — i.e. tortured or killed them.
views: Most modern translations read the Hebrew as forced labour with saws and picks, not torture
The difference turns on one Hebrew word in 1 Chronicles 20:3

items.title: Achan's family stoned and burned
items.what: For Achan's theft from Jericho, he, his sons and daughters and animals are stoned and burned.
views: Contrasts with Deut 24:16: children are not to die for a parent's sin
Corporate responsibility in ancient thought

items.title: Korah's households swallowed
items.what: The ground opens and swallows the rebels with their households and 'little children' (16:27).
views: Num 26:11 notes that Korah's sons did not die
Corporate judgment

items.title: Seven of Saul's sons executed to end a famine
items.what: David hands seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites, who hang them; the famine then ends.
views: Blood-guilt for Saul's breaking a treaty (Josh 9)
Rizpah's vigil over the bodies (21:10) moves David to bury them

items.title: 75,000 killed in the Persian provinces
items.what: The Jews, authorised by the king, kill those who planned to destroy them, including 75,000 in the provinces and Haman's ten sons.
views: Self-defence against a decreed genocide (Esth 3:13)
Origin of the feast of Purim

items.title: Blood up to the horses' bridles
items.what: Visions of final judgment: a winepress of wrath with blood flowing 1,600 furlongs, and birds summoned to eat the flesh of kings and armies.
views: Apocalyptic symbolism of judgment on evil
Critics note its violence toward enemies

items.title: The binding of Isaac
items.what: God tells Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a burnt offering; an angel stops him at the last moment.
views: A test of faith; the story ends with God forbidding the sacrifice
Read as a rejection of child sacrifice
Kierkegaard and others question a faith that obeys such a command

items.title: Jephthah's daughter
items.what: Jephthah vows to sacrifice whatever comes out of his house first if he wins; his daughter comes out, and 'he did with her according to his vow'.
views: Most read it as human sacrifice the narrator does not endorse
Some argue she was dedicated to lifelong virginity instead (11:37–39)
Hebrews 11:32 lists Jephthah among the faithful

items.title: The king of Moab sacrifices his son
items.what: Losing the battle, Moab's king offers his eldest son as a burnt offering on the wall, and 'there was great indignation against Israel', who withdraw.
views: Whose 'indignation' is meant — Moab's god, Israel's God, or the Moabites — is debated

items.title: "Statutes that were not good"
items.what: God says he gave Israel statutes that were not good and let them make their firstborn pass through the fire.
views: God handing people over to their own practices (compare Rom 1:24)
Others see a memory of firstborn sacrifice in Israel's past

items.title: Elisha and the bears
items.what: Youths mock Elisha; he curses them in the LORD's name and two bears maul forty-two of them.
views: The Hebrew can mean young men rather than small children (KJV 'little children')
A warning about contempt for a prophet

items.title: "Dasheth thy little ones against the stones"
items.what: An exile's psalm ends by blessing whoever will dash Babylon's infants against the rocks.
views: A raw cry of grief and rage from survivors of Jerusalem's destruction, voiced to God rather than acted on
Christian tradition often allegorised it; many lectionaries omit it

items.title: Infants dashed, pregnant women ripped open
items.what: Prophecies of conquest describe the killing of infants and pregnant women as judgment.
views: Describes the known brutality of Assyrian/Babylonian warfare as divine judgment

items.title: Mothers eating their children in siege
items.what: The covenant curses warn of, and later narratives report, parents eating their children during famine under siege.
views: Presented as the horror that follows covenant breaking

items.title: Beating a slave: "for he is his money"
items.what: A master who beats a slave to death is punished, but if the slave survives a day or two there is no punishment, 'for he is his money'.
views: One of the few ancient laws to punish killing a slave at all
Critics: treats a person as property; still permits beating

items.title: The slave's wife and children stay with the master
items.what: A Hebrew slave goes free after six years, but a wife and children given by the master remain the master's; to keep them he must become a slave for life.
views: Ancient debt-slavery regulated by term limits
Critics: the family is used as leverage

items.title: Selling a daughter as a servant
items.what: A man may sell his daughter as a maidservant (a concubine-wife); she does not go free like male slaves but has some protections.
views: Regulates a debt practice; requires food, clothing and marital rights or her release

items.title: Slaves from the nations, property forever
items.what: Israelites may buy slaves from surrounding nations and pass them on as an inheritance for ever; fellow Israelites are not to be treated so harshly.
views: Was cited in defence of American slavery
Distinguishes chattel slavery of foreigners from debt service of Israelites

items.title: "Servants, be obedient to your masters"
items.what: New Testament letters tell slaves to obey their masters, including harsh ones.
views: Also tells masters to treat slaves justly (Eph 6:9; Col 4:1) and urges Philemon to receive Onesimus 'as a brother'
Was quoted by both pro-slavery and abolitionist writers

items.title: Stoning a rebellious son
items.what: Parents may bring a stubborn, rebellious, drunken son to the elders, and the men of the city stone him.
views: Rabbinic tradition hedged it with so many conditions that it was said never to have been carried out
Removed the power of life and death from the father alone

items.title: Stoned for gathering sticks on the Sabbath
items.what: A man found gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned by the congregation at the LORD's command.
views: Presented as a test case for defiant sin (15:30–31)

items.title: Death penalties in Leviticus 20
items.what: Death is prescribed for cursing a parent, adultery, several kinds of incest, sex between men, and bestiality.
views: Holiness code for ancient Israel; Christians debate what still applies
Lev 20:13 is central to modern debates on homosexuality

items.title: Kill a relative who entices you to other gods
items.what: If a brother, child, spouse or friend secretly urges worship of other gods, you must not pity them; your hand is to be first in stoning them.
views: Treats apostasy as treason against the covenant
Cited historically in support of executing heretics

items.title: Cutting off a woman's hand
items.what: If a woman grabs the genitals of a man fighting her husband, her hand is to be cut off without pity.
views: The only bodily mutilation penalty in the Torah
Some scholars argue for a different reading of the penalty

items.title: Ananias and Sapphira
items.what: A couple lie about a gift to the church and each falls dead at Peter's words.
views: Judgment on deceiving the Holy Spirit in the founding community
Peter does not pronounce a sentence on Ananias, only exposes the lie

items.title: "Let the women learn in silence"
items.what: Women are told to be silent in the churches and not to teach or have authority over a man, with reference to Eve.
views: Addressed to specific local problems
Some argue 1 Cor 14:34–35 is a later insertion (it moves position in some manuscripts)
Others hold it as a lasting rule

items.title: The ordeal of the suspected wife
items.what: A wife suspected of adultery by a jealous husband must drink 'bitter water' before the priest; there is no matching test for husbands.
views: Removed punishment from the husband's hands to a ritual
Critics note the one-sided suspicion

items.title: The "curse of Ham"
items.what: Noah curses Canaan, Ham's son, to be a servant of servants to his brothers.
views: Was misused for centuries to justify enslaving Africans, though the text curses Canaan and says nothing about skin colour

items.title: "His blood be on us, and on our children"
items.what: The crowd before Pilate accepts responsibility for Jesus' death.
views: Was used for centuries to blame all Jews for Jesus' death and to justify persecution
Rejected by most churches today (e.g. Vatican II, Nostra Aetate)

items.title: "Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live"
items.what: A sorceress is to be put to death.
views: Quoted to justify the European and colonial witch trials
The Hebrew word refers to a practitioner of sorcery, not the later idea of witchcraft
